item.title: Distinct gradients of cortical architecture capture visual representations and behavior across the lifespan.
item.description:
eLife
The microstructure of cells within the human cerebral cortex varies across the cortical ribbon, where changes in cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture are thought to endow each region of the cortex with its unique function. While fine-scale relative to a cell, these changes at the population level impact architectural properties of the cortex measurable in vivo by noninvasive MRI, such as the thickness and myelin content of the cortex. This raises the question of whether or not we can use these in vivo architectural measures to understand cortical organization, function, and development more broadly. Using the human visual cortex as a test bed, we demonstrated two architectural gradients, one in which cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture converge and another in which they diverge. These two gradients underlie the structural and functional topography of the visual cortex, even predicting the presence of new visual representations. Moreover, the two gradients show distinct visual behavior relevance and lifespan trajectory. These findings provide a more general framework for understanding the human cortex, showing that architectural gradients are a measurable fingerprint of functional organization and ontogenetic routines in the human brain.

item.title: From Images and Words to Modality-Independent Semantic Representations: When and Where They Emerge
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Conceptual knowledge can be accessed from different modalities, such as seeing an image or reading a written word. While prior neuroimaging studies implicate anterior temporal cortex in modality-independent semantic representations, when and how representations evoked by images and words converge onto a modality-independent code remains unclear. Moreover, evidence for modality-independent category representations comes largely from tasks that explicitly required semantic processing, leaving open whether such representations emerge when semantic category and stimulus modality are task-irrelevant. We magnetoencephalography (MEG) to determine when and where modality-independent semantic category representations emerge across images and words when participants (n = 32) encoded six-item sequences containing an exemplar of six semantic categories counterbalanced across positions and reported the ordinal position of a probed item. Decoding performance was above chance for all categories in each modality from approximately 70 ms relative to item presentation. Generalization peaked at similar latencies for the two modalities (~520-530 ms), where image and word classifiers had the most similar coefficients. In both transfer directions, activity elicited by images generalized mostly to later activity elicited by words, and a given period of the image response shared its category code with a longer period of the word response. Source-space decoding around the peak of generalization identified the same regions for both transfer directions: left and right anterior temporal lobe, perisylvian cortex (more extensive in the left hemisphere), right visual cortex, and bilateral orbitofrontal cortex, indicating a modality-independent category code distributed across the cortex.

item.title: Full-Term and Preterm Differences in Human Brain Functional Connectivity Development Across Birth
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
We possess a limited understanding of how preterm and full-term brains develop during the earliest stages of life, from the fetal to neonatal period, and how they respond to the birth transition. Here, we characterize brain resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) using over 1000 longitudinal fetal and infant functional MRI scans from 21 to 52 post-conception weeks across birth. By mapping the developmental trajectory of RSFC across this window, we unveil marked divergences in developmental patterns between preterm- and term-born brains at both the global and network levels. When aligned by birth, the full-term group exhibit generally higher RSFC than the preterm group. For selected between-network connections with a significant prematurity effect, full-term cases demonstrate an overall increase in RSFC across age, whereas preterm cases show minimal change or even a decrease in connectivity of these systems. In contrast, when aligned by postconceptional age, the preterm group shows an accelerated increase in RSFC between 30 and 40 weeks. Across comparisons, mode of delivery and sex showed minimal influence on these trajectories. These findings offer novel insight into how prematurity and early exposure to the extrauterine environment alter the developmental trajectories of large-scale neural networks, advancing our understanding of both typical and preterm brain development.

item.title: Item-specific clustering of high gamma-band activity on theta phase during speech categorization
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) has been proposed as a mechanism for separating neural representations in time. Although item-specific PAC has been reported, its role in perception remains unclear. Notably, previous work has shown that theta phase can bias perception, raising the question whether such biases are linked to phase-specific gamma activity. Here, we investigated whether phase-dependent perceptual biases are accompanied by item-specific theta-gamma PAC. We presented ambiguous speech sounds that could be interpreted as either /da/ or /ga/ in patients with epilepsy implanted with intracranial electrocorticography. We found that pre-stimulus theta phase predicted both the neural and perceptual response, with /da/ and /ga/ tuned channels exhibiting gamma activity clustering at distinct theta phases. These findings suggest that neural and perceptual biases stem from phase-specific pre-activation of item-specific neural representations. They demonstrate the generalizability of the theta-gamma code, shaping behavior and enhancing representational capacity.

item.title: Decomposing Parts of Speech: Neural Encoding of Semantic and Grammatical Dimensions and Their Combinational Structure
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Conventional part-of-speech (PoS) labels such as nouns, verbs and adjectives conflate lexical-semantic roots, grammatical functions, and their combinations, making it unclear whether neural sensitivity to PoS reflects either dimension or the way they are combined. We adopted Croft's typological framework to decompose major PoS classes into semantic root type and grammatical function and define prototypical nouns, verbs, and adjectives through the prototypical mappings between semantic root and grammatical function. We fitted time-resolved encoding models to magnetoencephalography (MEG) data from three participants who each listened to approximately ten hours of narrative speech. We examined the unique predictive contributions of semantic root, grammatical function, their interaction, and a binary prototypicality predictor, and whether the three prototypes exhibited distinct neural response dynamics. Semantic root and grammatical function contributed independently to neural responses during naturalistic language comprehension, with additional contributions from their interaction beyond the main effects. Root effects were predominantly left-lateralized, function effects were more bilateral, and interaction effects were concentrated in the left temporal and temporoparietal cortex, with overlap in left temporal regions. Further analyses revealed significant neural sensitivity to the distinction between prototypical and nonprototypical combinations in two of the three datasets. Prototypical nouns and verbs showed distinct coefficient time courses in all three participants, most consistently in left superior temporal cortex, whereas adjective-related contrasts were less consistent. These within-participant findings support a decompositional account of neural word-class sensitivity involving semantic, grammatical, and the mappings between them within distributed, partially overlapping cortical networks.

item.title: Salience network expansion as a transdiagnostic neural marker for psychopathology risk in adolescence
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Increased cortical surface area of the brain's salience network (SAL) has been observed in depression and appears to emerge during early adolescence. However, similar expansion has also been reported in bipolar disorder (BD), obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD), and other atypicalities of salience network function have been broadly implicated across multiple psychiatric conditions. Whether increased SAL surface area is specific to depression or related more generally with psychopathology remains unclear. Using data collected as part of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (baseline: N = 7942; ages 9-10; Year 2: N = 5901; ages 11-12), we quantified individual SAL size and examined associations with dimensional symptoms from the Child Behavior Checklist. SAL surface area showed substantial inter-individual variability, with expansion occurring primarily through encroachment into the default mode (DMN), action-mode (AMN), and frontoparietal (FP) networks. Larger SAL size showed a modest positive association with depressive symptoms in the baseline sample, consistent with prior reports; however, this association did not replicate in the year 2 internal replication sample. Instead, associations with total problems were stronger and replicated across both timepoints, suggesting a subtle, dimensional relationship between SAL organization and general psychopathology burden. These findings suggest that individual differences in SAL organization may represent a broader transdiagnostic neural correlate of dimensional psychopathology rather than a disorder-specific neural signature.

item.title: Algorithmic Geometry Shapes the Biological Meaning of Thalamocortical Structural Covariance
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Neuroimaging studies often derive and discuss structural covariance (SC) as a representation of underlying brain circuitry that reflects coordinated maturation, anatomical connectivity, transcriptional similarity, and shared genetic influences. These associations motivate its use to study brain organization across development, aging, and disease. However, the algorithms used to derive SC networks impose constraints that may shape their biological interpretation. To understand the impact of algorithm choice, we used the thalamocortical system as an example and compared five common representations of voxelwise SC, namely, principal component analysis (PCA), independent component analysis (ICA), non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), orthogonal projective NMF (OPNMF), and \textit{k}-means clustering, in 755 participants aged 8--22 years from the Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort (PNC). SC networks derived from deformation-based morphometry (DBM) were evaluated against three complementary biological benchmarks: age-related individual differences, fractional-anisotropy (FA)-based microstructural connectivity of regionally-specific thalamocortical connections, and Allen Human Brain Atlas gene expression. Each algorithm demonstrated underlying sensitivity to differing aspects of neurobiology: PCA and OPNMF showed the strongest associations between participant-level component weights and age. NMF, OPNMF, and \textit{k}-means showed greater spatial overlap between positive cortical SC and tractography-derived projections. ICA and PCA showed stronger correspondence between thalamic and cortical gene-expression profiles across the transcriptome, whereas NMF, OPNMF, and \textit{k}-means more often identified thalamic components with relatively high core-matrix gene expression. This study emphasizes that algorithmic constraints effectively act as biological priors and decomposition methods do not provide neutral compression of the data. We conclude that it is critical to consider whether the algorithmic objective matches the representational geometry of the neurobiology being studied. Overall, our findings suggest that SC studies should select and justify algorithms according to the biological question, explicitly considering whether their constraints favour distributed gradients, overlapping regional parts, or discrete clusters. Meanwhile, interpretations of SC findings could also be informed by the specific algorithmic constraints used to derive them.

item.title: Behavioral Markers of Essential Tremor Correlate with Distributed Alteration of Brain Functional Connectivity
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Essential Tremor (ET) is a common motor disorder characterized by involuntary oscillations of the upper limbs during voluntary movement. Although increasing evidence implicates dysfunction of the cerebello-thalamo-cortical pathway, ET remains a diagnosis of exclusion, as no definitive biological marker currently exists. To better characterize ET, we recently hypothesized that impaired compensation of sensorimotor delays within the long-latency feedback pathways may generate the tremor-like oscillations observed in ET. This theory suggests that the mean spectral amplitude (MSA), derived from limb kinematics, may serve as a potential marker of ET. Here we investigated the relationship between MSA, standard clinical assessment (Fahn Tolosa Marin Tremor Rating Scale; FTM-TRS), and brain connectivity derived from resting state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI). Using seed-based analyses, we replicated previous findings of reduced functional connectivity between the dentate nucleus and components of the cerebello-thalamo-cortical pathway in ET patients compared with neurologically intact (NI) age-matched participants. Graph-theoretical analyses of whole-brain functional networks revealed distributed alterations in network topology across motor-related cortical and subcortical regions. Several graph metrics correlated with FTM-TRS scores and/or MSA, particularly within motor-related cortical and subcortical circuits, including the thalamus, basal ganglia, and cerebellum in ET. These findings indicate that ET is characterized by distributed alterations in functional brain networks beyond reduced connectivity of dentate nucleus and highlights MSA as a candidate quantitative marker linking altered brain connectivity to sensorimotor delay-driven tremor oscillations.

item.title: Pre-stress functional brain connectivity is associated with subsequent anxiety during war-related stress
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Individuals exposed to major real-world stressors show markedly different psychological outcomes, but whether this heterogeneity is associated with pre-existing neural characteristics remains unclear because neuroimaging is rarely performed beforehand. We acquired resting-state fMRI in healthy adults before the unforeseen onset of war-related stress. Approximately 13 months later, during ongoing war-related stress, participants (n = 31) were assessed for anxiety, depressive symptoms, perceived stress and post-traumatic stress symptoms. Among 144 associations spanning 36 predefined corticolimbic and reward-related connections and four outcomes, lower baseline functional connectivity between the right nucleus accumbens and right amygdala was associated with greater subsequent anxiety. This association survived permutation-based family-wise error correction and adjustment for baseline depressive symptoms, age and sex. These findings provide preliminary prospective evidence that pre-existing functional organization of threat- and reward-related circuitry is associated with individual differences in anxiety during prolonged adversity.

item.title: Constantin von Economo (1876-1931): cytoarchitectonic roots of modern network neuroscience.
item.description:
Journal of neurosurgery
Constantin von Economo (1876-1931) is widely remembered for his seminal description of encephalitis lethargica, yet his broader contribution to cortical organization remains underappreciated. Beyond clinical neurology, von Economo and Georg Koskinas, a neurologist-psychiatrist, contributed to the broader cytoarchitectonic tradition by developing one of the most detailed architectonic frameworks of the human cerebral cortex, emphasizing laminar heterogeneity, regional transition, and structural specialization. These concepts can be reconsidered in relation to contemporary models of large-scale brain organization. In particular, cortical territories associated with von Economo's work, including the anterior insula and anterior cingulate region, are now recognized as key hubs in salience processing and contain the distinctive spindle-shaped neurons later termed von Economo neurons. Recent advances in connectomics, cortical gradient mapping, and laminar neuroimaging have renewed interest in the relationship between cortical microstructure and distributed functional networks. From this perspective, von Economo's work may be viewed not simply as a landmark in classical neuroanatomy, but as a historically important structural framework that can be reinterpreted in relation to modern ideas of structure-function coupling and network-level brain organization. This historical vignette revisits his life, scientific contributions, and enduring relevance to contemporary neuroscience and neurosurgical thinking.

item.title: Interpretable embeddings of speech explain and enhance the brain encoding performance of audio models.
item.description:
PLoS computational biology
Speech foundation models (SFMs) are increasingly hailed as powerful computational models of human speech perception. However, since their representations are inherently black-box, it remains unclear what drives their alignment with brain responses. To remedy this, we built linear encoding models from six interpretable feature families: mel-spectrogram, Gabor filter bank features, speech presence, phonetic, syntactic, and semantic features, and contextualized embeddings from three state-of-the-art SFMs (Whisper, HuBERT, WavLM), quantifying electrocorticography (ECoG) response variance shared between feature classes. Variance-partitioning analyses revealed several key insights: First, the SFMs' alignment with the brain can be mostly accounted for by their ability to learn and encode simple interpretable speech features. Second, SFMs exhibit a systematic trade-off between encoding of brain-relevant low-level and high-level features across layers. Finally, our results show that SFMs learn brain-relevant semantics which cannot be accounted for by lower-level speech features, with this capacity increasing with model size and context length. Together, our findings suggest a principled approach to build more interpretable, accurate, and efficient encoding models of the brain by augmenting SFM embeddings with interpretable features.
